paragraphs: Until now I have treated each State as a separate whole, and I have explained the various springs the people sets in motion and the various means of action it uses. But all the States I have treated as independent must, in certain cases, submit to the supreme authority of the Union. The time has now come to examine separately the supremacy the Union has been given, and to take a quick look at the Federal Constitution.
Origin of the first Union — Its weakness — Congress appeals to the constituent authority — Two years pass between this appeal and the announcement of the new Constitution.
History of the Federal Constitution

The thirteen colonies that threw off the English yoke at the same moment, toward the end of the last century, had, as I have already observed, the same religion, the same language, the same customs, and almost the same laws. They were fighting a common enemy. These reasons were strong enough to unite them with one another and to consolidate them into one nation. But each colony had enjoyed a separate existence and a government under its own control, and the particular interests and customs that this system produced stood against a close and intimate union, which would have absorbed the individual importance of each into the general importance of all. Hence two opposite tendencies arose: one urged the Anglo-Americans to unite, the other to divide their strength. As long as the war with the mother country lasted, necessity kept the principle of union alive. The laws that established it were defective, yet the common tie held in spite of their flaws. *a But as soon as peace was concluded, the faults of the legislation became obvious, and the State seemed to dissolve all at once. Each colony became an independent republic and claimed absolute sovereignty. The Federal government had been condemned to impotence by its constitution, and a common danger no longer supported it. It witnessed the outrages offered to its flag by the great nations of Europe, and it could scarcely hold its ground against the Native American tribes or pay the interest on the debt contracted during the war of independence. It was already on the verge of collapse when it officially declared that it could not govern and appealed to the constituent authority of the nation. *b If America ever came near (however briefly) to that lofty pinnacle of glory to which its inhabitants like to point in their imagination, it was at the solemn moment when the power of the nation, so to speak, gave up its rule over the land. Every age has offered the spectacle of a people struggling vigorously to win its independence, and the efforts of the Americans in throwing off the English yoke have been greatly exaggerated. They were separated from their enemies by three thousand miles of ocean and backed by a powerful ally. The success of the United States may more fairly be credited to their geographical position than to the valor of their armies or the patriotism of their citizens. It would be ridiculous to compare the American war with the wars of the French Revolution, or the efforts of the Americans with those of the French. The French were attacked by the whole of Europe, without credit and without allies, and yet they were able to set a twentieth part of their population against the world, and to carry the torch of revolution beyond their frontiers while they smothered its devouring flame at home. But it is a novelty in the history of society to see a great people turn a calm and searching eye on itself when the legislature informs it that the wheels of government have stopped. It examines the extent of the evil with care and waits patiently for two whole years until a remedy is found, and it then adopts that remedy of its own free will, without having wrung a tear or a drop of blood from mankind. When the inadequacy of the first constitution was discovered, America had a double advantage: the calm that had followed the excitement of the revolution, and the great men who had led the revolution to a successful end. The assembly that took on the task of composing the second constitution was small, *c but George Washington was its President, and it held the finest talents and the noblest hearts the New World had ever produced. After long and careful deliberation, this national commission offered the people the body of general laws that still governs the Union. All the States adopted it one after another. *d The new Federal government began its functions in 1789, after an interregnum of two years. The American Revolution ended when the French Revolution began.

a [ See the articles of the first confederation formed in 1778. This constitution was not adopted by all the States until 1781. See also the analysis given of this constitution in “The Federalist” from No. 15 to No. 22, inclusive, and Story’s “Commentaries on the Constitution of the United States,” pp. 85-115.]
b [ Congress made this declaration on February 21, 1787.]
c [ It consisted of fifty-five members; Washington, Madison, Hamilton, and the two Morrises were among them.]

d [ It was not adopted by the legislative bodies. Instead, representatives were elected by the people for this one purpose, and the new constitution was discussed at length in each of these assemblies.]
Summary of the Federal Constitution
Division of authority between the Federal government and the States — The government of the States is the rule, the Federal government the exception.

The first question facing the Americans was intricate and by no means easy to solve. The aim was to divide the authority of the different States that made up the Union in such a way that each State would keep governing itself in everything that concerned its internal prosperity, while the entire nation, represented by the Union, would keep forming a compact body and would provide for the general needs of the people. It was as impossible to determine in advance, with any accuracy, the share of authority each of two governments would have as it was to foresee every incident in the life of a nation.

The obligations and claims of the Federal government were simple and easy to define, because the Union had been formed expressly to meet the general needs of the people. The claims and obligations of the States, on the other hand, were complicated and varied, because their governments had reached into every detail of social life. The powers of the Federal government were therefore carefully listed, and everything not included among them was declared to belong to the privileges of the several State governments. Thus the government of the States remained the rule, and that of the Confederation became the exception. *e
e [ See the Amendment to the Federal Constitution; “Federalist,” No. 32; Story, p. 711; Kent’s “Commentaries,” vol. i. p. 364.

It should be observed that whenever the Constitution does not reserve to Congress the exclusive right to regulate certain matters, the States may take up the matter until it is brought before the National Assembly. For instance, Congress has the right to make a general law on bankruptcy, but it neglects to do so. Each State is then free to make a law for itself. This point has been settled by argument in the law courts, and it may be said to belong more properly to jurisprudence.]

But it was foreseen that in practice questions might arise about the exact limits of this exceptional authority, and that it would be dangerous to submit such questions to the ordinary courts of justice, which the States themselves had set up in the States. A high Federal court was therefore created, *f whose purpose, among other functions, was to maintain the balance of power the Constitution had established between the two rival governments. *g
f [ The action of this court is indirect, as we shall show later.]

g [ This is how “The Federalist,” No. 45, explains the division of supremacy between the Union and the States: “The powers delegated by the Constitution to the Federal Government are few and defined. Those which are to remain in the State Governments are numerous and indefinite. The former will be exercised principally on external objects, as war, peace, negotiation, and foreign commerce. The powers reserved to the several States will extend to all the objects which, in the ordinary course of affairs, concern the internal order and prosperity of the State.” I shall often have occasion to quote “The Federalist” in this work. When the bill that has since become the Constitution of the United States was submitted to the people for approval, and the discussions were still going on, three men formed an association to explain to the nation the advantages of the proposed measure. They had already won a share of the fame they have enjoyed since: John Jay, Hamilton, and Madison. To this end they published a series of articles in the form of a journal, and the articles now make up a complete treatise. They called their journal “The Federalist,” and the name has stayed with the work. “The Federalist” is an excellent book, which ought to be familiar to the statesmen of every country, although it concerns America in particular.]
Prerogative of the Federal Government

The power to declare war, make peace, and levy general taxes belongs to the Federal government — What part of the country’s internal policy it may direct — In some respects the government of the Union is more centralized than the King’s government in the old French monarchy.

A people’s external relations can be compared to those of private individuals, and they cannot be managed well without a single head of government. The Union was therefore given the exclusive right to make peace and war, to conclude commercial treaties, to raise armies, and to equip fleets. *h The need for a national government was felt less urgently in directing the internal policy of society, but there are certain general interests that only a general authority can serve well. The Union was given the power to control the monetary system, to run the post office, and to open the great roads that were to connect the different parts of the country. *i The independence of each State’s government within its own sphere was formally recognized. Nevertheless, the Federal government was authorized to interfere in the internal affairs of the States *j in a few predetermined cases, in which a reckless abuse of their independence might endanger the security of the Union as a whole. Thus all the republics kept the power to modify and change their legislation at will, but they were forbidden to pass ex post facto laws or to create a class of nobles in their communities. *k Finally, since the Federal government had to be able to meet its obligations, it was given an unlimited power to levy taxes. *l
h [ See Constitution, sect. 8; “Federalist,” Nos. 41 and 42; Kent’s “Commentaries,” vol. i. p. 207; Story, pp. 358-382; Ibid. pp. 409-426.]

i [ Several other privileges of the same kind exist, such as the one that empowers the Union to legislate on bankruptcy, to grant patents, and to act in other matters where its intervention is clearly necessary.]
j [ Even in these cases its interference is indirect. The Union interferes by means of the tribunals, as will be shown later.]
k [ Federal Constitution, sect. 10, art. I.]
l [ Constitution, sects. 8, 9, and 10; “Federalist,” Nos. 30-36, inclusive, and 41-44; Kent’s “Commentaries,” vol. i. pp. 207 and 381; Story, pp. 329 and 514.]

Look at the balance of power the Federal Constitution established. On one side is the portion of sovereignty reserved to the several States; on the other is the share of power the Union has taken. It is plain that the Federal legislators had the clearest and most accurate ideas about the nature of centralization of government. The United States form not only a republic but a confederation. Nevertheless, the authority of the nation was more centralized than it was in several European monarchies when the American Constitution was framed. Take, for instance, the following two examples.

France had thirteen supreme courts of justice, which, generally speaking, had the right to interpret the law without appeal. The provinces called pays d’états were authorized to refuse their assent to a tax levied by the sovereign who represented the nation. In the Union there is only one tribunal to interpret the laws, just as there is only one legislature to make them, and a tax voted by the representatives of the nation binds all the citizens. On these two essential points, therefore, the Union exercises more central authority than the French monarchy possessed, although the Union is only an assemblage of confederate republics.

In Spain, certain provinces had the right to set up a system of customs duties of their own, although by its very nature that privilege belongs to national sovereignty. In America, Congress alone has the right to regulate the commercial relations of the States. In this respect, then, the government of the Confederation is more centralized than the kingdom of Spain. It is true that the power of the Crown in France or in Spain could always obtain by force whatever the country’s constitution denied it, and that the final result was therefore the same. But here I am discussing the theory of the Constitution.
Once the limits within which the Federal government was to act had been settled, the next point was to determine what powers it was to exercise.
Legislative Powers *m
m [ [In this chapter the author points out the essence of the conflict between the seceding States and the Union which caused the Civil War of 1861.]]

Division of the legislative body into two branches — Difference in the way the two Houses are formed — The principle of the independence of the States prevails in forming the Senate — The principle of the sovereignty of the nation prevails in composing the House of Representatives — Odd effects of the fact that a constitution can be logical only in the early stages of a nation.

The plan laid down earlier for the Constitutions of the several States was followed, on many points, in organizing the powers of the Union. The Federal legislature of the Union was composed of a Senate and a House of Representatives. A spirit of conciliation required that different principles be followed in forming these two assemblies. I have already shown that two opposed interests clashed when the Federal Constitution was established. These two interests had given rise to two opinions. One party wished to turn the Union into a league of independent States, or a kind of congress where the representatives of the several peoples would meet to discuss certain points of common interest. The other party wished to unite the inhabitants of the American colonies into a single nation and to set up a government that would act as the sole representative of the nation, as far as the limited sphere of its authority allowed. The practical consequences of these two theories were very different.

The question was whether a league was to be established in place of a national government, and whether the majority of the States, rather than the majority of the inhabitants of the Union, was to make the law. In that case every State, small or great, would keep the full enjoyment of its independence and would enter the Union on a footing of perfect equality. If, however, the inhabitants of the United States were to be regarded as belonging to one and the same nation, it would be just for the majority of the citizens of the Union to prescribe the law. Of course the smaller States could not accept this doctrine without in fact giving up their existence in relation to the sovereignty of the Confederation, since they would have gone from being a co-equal and co-legislative authority to being an insignificant fraction of a great people. If the first system would have given them excessive authority, the second would have wiped out their influence altogether. In these circumstances the strict rules of logic were evaded, as usually happens when interests are opposed to arguments. The legislators found a middle course, which forced together two systems that in theory could not be reconciled.

The principle of the independence of the States prevailed in forming the Senate, and the principle of the sovereignty of the nation prevailed in composing the House of Representatives. It was decided that each State should send two senators to Congress, and a number of representatives in proportion to its population. *n The result of this arrangement is that the State of New York today has forty representatives and only two senators, while the State of Delaware has two senators and only one representative. Delaware is therefore equal to New York in the Senate, while New York has forty times Delaware’s influence in the House of Representatives. Thus, if a minority of the nation prevails in the Senate, it may paralyze the decisions of the majority represented in the other House, which is contrary to the spirit of constitutional government.

n [ Every ten years Congress fixes anew the number of representatives each State is to send. The total number was 69 in 1789, and 240 in 1833. (See “American Almanac,” 1834, p. 194.) The Constitution decided that there should not be more than one representative for every 30,000 persons, but it set no minimum. Congress has not thought fit to increase the number of representatives in proportion to the growth of population. The first Act passed on the subject (April 14, 1792: see “Laws of the United States,” by Story, vol. i. p. 235) decided that there should be one representative for every 33,000 inhabitants. The last Act, passed in 1832, fixes the proportion at one for 48,000. The population represented is made up of all the free men and of three-fifths of the slaves.

[The last Act of apportionment, passed February 2, 1872, fixes the representation at one to 134,684 inhabitants. There are now (1875) 283 members of the lower House of Congress, and 9 for the States at large, making in all 292 members. The old States have of course lost the representatives which the new States have gained.—Translator’s Note.]]

These facts show how rare and how difficult it is to combine all the parts of a legislative system in a rational and logical way. In the course of time, different interests arise and the same people approves different principles. When a general constitution has to be established, these interests and principles are so many natural obstacles to the rigorous application of any political system with all its consequences. Only in the early stages of national existence is it possible to keep the logic of legislation complete. When we see a nation enjoying this advantage, we should remember, before we hurry to conclude that it is wise, that it is young. When the Federal Constitution was formed, the interest of independence for the separate States and the interest of union for the whole people were the only two conflicting interests among the Anglo-Americans, and a compromise between them was inevitable.

It is only fair to acknowledge, however, that so far this part of the Constitution has not produced the evils that might have been feared. All the States are young and neighboring; their customs, their ideas, and their needs are not dissimilar; and the differences that come from their size or smallness are not enough to set their interests at odds. The small States have therefore never been led to band together in the Senate against the designs of the larger ones. Indeed, the legitimate expression of the will of a people carries such irresistible authority that the Senate could offer only feeble opposition to the vote of the majority of the House of Representatives.

It must not be forgotten, on the other hand, that it was not in the power of the American legislators to reduce to a single nation the people for whom they were making laws. The object of the Federal Constitution was not to destroy the independence of the States but to restrain it. By acknowledging the real authority of these secondary communities (and it was impossible to deprive them of it), the legislators disavowed in advance any habitual use of force to carry out the decisions of the majority. On this principle there was nothing surprising in bringing the influence of the States into the machinery of the Federal government. It merely attested the existence of a recognized power, which had to be handled with tact and not forcibly checked.
A Further Difference Between the Senate and the House of Representatives

The Senate is named by the legislatures of the States, the Representatives by the people — The former are elected twice over, the latter once — Term of the different offices — The particular functions of each House.

The Senate differs from the other House not only in the principle it represents but also in the way it is elected, in the term for which it is chosen, and in the nature of its functions. The House of Representatives is named by the people, the Senate by the legislators of each State. The former is elected directly, the latter by an elected body. Representatives are chosen for only two years, senators for six. The functions of the House of Representatives are purely legislative, and its only share in the judicial power is the impeachment of public officials. The Senate cooperates in the work of legislation, and it tries those political offenses that the House of Representatives submits to its decision. It also acts as the great executive council of the nation. Treaties concluded by the President must be ratified by the Senate, and the appointments he makes must be finally approved by the same body. *o
o [ See “The Federalist,” Nos. 52-56, inclusive; Story, pp. 199-314; Constitution of the United States, sects. 2 and 3.] The Executive Power *p
p [ See “The Federalist,” Nos. 67-77; Constitution of the United States, art. 2; Story, p. 315, pp. 615-780; Kent’s “Commentaries,” p. 255.]

Dependence of the President — He is elected and answerable — He is free to act in his own sphere under the inspection, but not the direction, of the Senate — His salary is fixed when he enters office — Suspensive veto.

The American legislators took on a difficult task when they tried to create an executive power that would depend on the majority of the people and yet be strong enough to act without restraint in its own sphere. To preserve the republican form of government, it was essential that the representative of the executive power be subject to the will of the nation.

The President is an elected magistrate. His honor, his property, his liberty, and his life are the guarantees the people holds that he will use his power with moderation. But in exercising his authority he cannot be called perfectly independent. The Senate takes notice of his relations with foreign powers and of how he distributes public appointments, so that he can neither be bribed nor use the means of corruption himself. The legislators of the Union recognized that the executive power could not carry out its task with dignity and usefulness unless it had greater stability and strength than it had been given in the separate States.

The President is chosen for four years and may be reelected. The prospect of a long administration may thus inspire him with hopeful undertakings for the public good, and give him the means of carrying them out. The President was made the sole representative of the executive power of the Union, and care was taken not to make his decisions subject to the vote of a council. That would have been a dangerous measure, which tends both to clog the action of the government and to reduce its responsibility. The Senate has the right to annul certain acts of the President, but it cannot compel him to take any step, nor does it share in the exercise of the executive power.

The legislature’s action on the executive power may be direct, and we have just shown that the Americans carefully prevented this influence. But it may also be indirect. Public assemblies that have the power to deprive an officer of state of his salary encroach on his independence. And since they are free to make the laws, there is reason to fear that they may gradually take for themselves a portion of the authority the Constitution placed in his hands. This dependence of the executive power is one of the defects inherent in republican constitutions. The Americans have not been able to counteract the tendency of legislative assemblies to take possession of the government, but they have made this tendency less irresistible. The President’s salary is fixed, when he enters office, for the whole period of his magistracy. The President is also given a suspensive veto, which allows him to oppose the passing of laws that might destroy the portion of independence the Constitution grants him. The struggle between the President and the legislature must always be an unequal one, since the legislature is certain to overcome all resistance if it persists in its plans. But the suspensive veto at least forces it to reconsider the matter, and if it persists in the motion, the motion must then be backed by a majority of two-thirds of the whole house. The veto is, in fact, a kind of appeal to the people. Without this security, the executive power might have been oppressed in secret. By the veto it pleads its cause and states its reasons. Suppose someone objects that the legislature is certain to overcome all resistance by persisting in its plans. I reply that in the constitutions of all nations, of whatever kind, there is a certain point at which the legislator must rely on the good sense and the virtue of his fellow citizens. This point is more prominent and easier to find in republics, and more remote and more carefully hidden in monarchies, but it always exists somewhere. There is no country in the world where everything can be provided for by the laws, or where political institutions can take the place of common sense and public morality.
Differences Between the Position of the President of the United States and That of a Constitutional King of France

Executive power in the Northern States is as limited and partial as the supremacy it represents — Executive power in France is as universal as the supremacy it represents — The King is a branch of the legislature — The President is the mere executor of the law — Other differences arising from the duration of the two powers — The President is checked in exercising executive authority — The King is independent in exercising it — Despite these differences, France is more akin to a republic than the Union is to a monarchy — Comparison of the number of public officials who depend on the executive power in the two countries.

The executive power has so important an influence on the destinies of nations that I am inclined to pause for a moment on this part of my subject, in order to explain more clearly the part it plays in America. To form an accurate idea of the position of the President of the United States, it may be useful to compare it with that of one of the constitutional kings of Europe. In this comparison I shall pay little attention to the outward signs of power, which are more apt to mislead the observer than to guide his inquiry. When a monarchy is gradually transformed into a republic, the executive power keeps the titles, the honors, the etiquette, and even the funds of royalty long after its authority has disappeared. The English cut off the head of one king and drove another from his throne, and yet they were used to approaching the successor of those princes on their knees. On the other hand, when a republic falls under the sway of a single individual, the sovereign’s bearing is simple and unpretending, as if his authority were not yet supreme. When the emperors had unlimited control over the fortunes and the lives of their fellow citizens, it was customary to call them Caesar in conversation, and they were in the habit of dining informally at their friends’ houses. It is therefore necessary to look beneath the surface.

Sovereignty in the United States is shared between the Union and the States, while in France it is undivided and compact. From this arises the first and most notable difference between the President of the United States and the King of France. In the United States the executive power is as limited and partial as the sovereignty of the Union in whose name it acts. In France it is as universal as the authority of the state. The Americans have a federal government and the French a national government.

This cause of inferiority results from the nature of things, but it is not the only one. The second in importance is as follows. Sovereignty may be defined as the right to make laws. In France the King really exercises a portion of the sovereign power, since the laws have no force until he has given his assent to them. He is, moreover, the executor of everything they ordain. The President is also the executor of the laws, but he does not really take part in making them, since his refusal of assent does not annul them. He is therefore to be considered merely as the agent of the sovereign power. But the King of France not only exercises a portion of the sovereign power; he also helps to name the legislature, which exercises the other portion. He has the privilege of appointing the members of one chamber and of dissolving the other at his pleasure. The President of the United States has no share in forming the legislative body and cannot dissolve any part of it. The King has the same right as the Chambers to bring forward measures, a right the President does not have. The King is represented in each assembly by his ministers, who explain his intentions, support his opinions, and defend the principles of the government. The President and his ministers are alike excluded from Congress, so that his influence and his opinions can reach that great body only indirectly. The King of France therefore stands on an equal footing with the legislature, which can no more act without him than he can without it. The President exercises an authority that is inferior to that of the legislature and depends on it.

Even in exercising the executive power properly so called, the point on which his position seems most like that of the King of France, the President labors under several causes of inferiority. First, the authority of the King in France has the advantage of duration over that of the President, and durability is one of the chief elements of strength. People love or fear only what is likely to last. The President of the United States is a magistrate elected for four years; the King of France is a hereditary sovereign. In exercising the executive power, the President of the United States is constantly under jealous scrutiny. He may negotiate a treaty but cannot conclude it; he may nominate a public official but cannot appoint him. *q The King of France is absolute within the limits of his authority. The President of the United States is answerable for his actions, but the person of the King is declared inviolable by the French Charter. *r

q [ The Constitution had left it doubtful whether the President was obliged to consult the Senate in removing as well as in appointing Federal officers. “The Federalist” (No. 77) seemed to establish that he was. But in 1789 Congress formally decided that, since the President was responsible for his actions, he ought not to be forced to employ agents who had lost his esteem. See Kent’s “Commentaries”, vol. i. p. 289.]
r [ [This comparison applied to the Constitutional King of France and to the powers he held under the Charter of 1830, till the overthrow of the monarchy in 1848.—Translator’s Note.]]

Nevertheless, the supremacy of public opinion stands over the head of the one no less than over the other. This power is less definite, less evident, and less backed by the laws in France than in America, but in fact it exists. In America it acts through elections and decrees; in France it proceeds by revolutions. But despite the different constitutions of the two countries, public opinion is the dominant authority in both. The fundamental principle of legislation, a principle essentially republican, is the same in both countries, although its consequences may differ and its results may be more or less far-reaching. From this I am led to conclude that France with its King is nearer to being a republic than the Union with its President is to being a monarchy.

In what I have been saying I have touched only on the main points of difference. If I could have gone into details, the contrast would have been even more striking. I have observed that the authority of the President in the United States is exercised only within the limits of a partial sovereignty, while that of the King in France is undivided. I could go on to show that the power of the King’s government in France goes beyond its natural limits, wide as they are, and reaches in a thousand different ways into the management of private interests. One example of this influence is the great number of public officials, all of whom owe their appointments to the government. This number now exceeds all previous limits; it comes to 138,000 *s nominations, each of which may be regarded as an element of power. The President of the United States has no exclusive right to make any public appointments, and their whole number scarcely exceeds 12,000. *t
s [ The sums annually paid by the State to these officers amount to 200,000,000 fr. ($40,000,000).]

t [ This number is extracted from the “National Calendar” for 1833. The “National Calendar” is an American almanac that contains the names of all the Federal officers. The comparison shows that the King of France has eleven times as many places at his disposal as the President, although the population of France is not much more than double that of the Union.

[I have no means of finding out the number of appointments now at the disposal of the President of the United States, but his patronage and the abuse of it have greatly increased since 1833.—Translator’s Note, 1875.]]
Accidental Causes That May Increase the Influence of the Executive Government
External security of the Union — An army of six thousand men — Few ships — The President has no opportunity to exercise his great prerogatives — In the prerogatives he does exercise he is weak.
If the executive government is weaker in America than in France, the cause lies more in circumstances than in the laws of the country.

It is chiefly in its foreign relations that the executive power of a nation is called on to show its skill and its vigor. If the existence of the Union were constantly threatened, and if its chief interests were in daily contact with those of other powerful nations, the executive government would grow in importance in proportion to what was expected of it and to what it carried out. The President of the United States is commander-in-chief of the army, but of an army of only six thousand men. He commands the fleet, but the fleet has only a few ships. He conducts the foreign relations of the Union, but the United States is a nation without neighbors. Separated from the rest of the world by the ocean, and still too weak to aim at dominion over the seas, the United States has no enemies, and its interests rarely come into contact with those of any other nation on the globe.

The practical working of a government must not be judged by the theory of its constitution. The President of the United States possesses almost royal prerogatives, which he has no opportunity to exercise. The privileges he can use at present are very limited. The laws allow him a degree of influence that circumstances do not let him employ.

On the other hand, the great strength of the royal prerogative in France comes far more from circumstances than from the laws. There the executive government is constantly struggling against enormous obstacles and straining all its energies to overcome them. It therefore grows with the extent of its achievements and the importance of the events it controls, without any change in its constitution. If the laws had made it as weak and as limited as it is in the Union, its influence would very soon become still more dominant.
